hints: Think about what makes $\bullet\text{NH}_2$ and $\bullet\text{Cl}$ different from normal stable molecules in terms of electron pairing.
walkthrough:
Picture a normal covalent bond**
In a stable molecule every electron is normally paired up in a bond or a lone pair. A free radical is formed when a bond splits evenly, homolytic fission, so each fragment keeps just one electron from the pair.
Final answer: A species with an unpaired electron.

hints: Recall that the step shown consumes one radical and makes a new one, so consider what type of radical-radical combination would remove radicals completely.
walkthrough:
Sort propagation from termination**
The step $\text{NH}_2\text{Cl} + \bullet\text{Cl} \rightarrow \bullet\text{NHCl} + \text{HCl}$ starts with one radical and ends with a different radical, so radicals are conserved. That is propagation. Termination must do the opposite and destroy radicals.

Combine two radicals**
Join any two radicals from the initiation step together with no unpaired electrons left over: $\bullet\text{NH}_2 + \bullet\text{Cl} \rightarrow \text{NH}_2\text{Cl}$. Both unpaired electrons pair up to make a new $\text{N-Cl}$ bond.

hints: Count valence electrons for N (5), each H (1) and Cl (7), then arrange three single bonds around N leaving one lone pair to complete the octet.
walkthrough:
Build the skeleton**
Put N in the centre with H, H and Cl around it. Each single bond is one shared pair, use crosses for H and Cl electrons and dots for N electrons, for example.

Complete the octets**
N already has three bonding pairs, so add one lone pair (two dots) to give 8 electrons around N. Cl has one bonding pair, so add three lone pairs to give 8 electrons around Cl. H atoms need only the single bonding pair.

Final answer: Dot-cross diagram of $\text{NH}_2\text{Cl}$ with central N bonded to $2 \times \text{H}$ and $1 \times \text{Cl}$ by single bonds, one lone pair on N and three lone pairs on Cl, outer electrons only shown.

hints: Count sigma bonds plus lone pairs on N in $\text{NH}_2\text{Cl}$ and link this electron domain number to hybridisation and to the ammonia-like shape.
walkthrough:
Count electron domains on N**
N has three $\sigma$ bonds ($2 \times \text{N-H}$, $1 \times \text{N-Cl}$) plus one lone pair, four domains in total. Four domains means tetrahedral electron geometry, which comes from $\text{sp}^3$ hybridisation.

Allow for lone pair squeeze**
The molecular shape is trigonal pyramidal like $\text{NH}_3$. The lone pair repels more strongly than bonding pairs, squeezing the angle below the ideal $109.5^{\circ}$ to about $107^{\circ}$ or slightly less, so accept $100-107^{\circ}$.
Final answer: hybridisation of N: $\text{sp}^3$; $\text{H-N-Cl}$ bond angle: $100-107^{\circ}$

hints: Think of entropy as a count of how many ways particles and energy can be arranged, linking it to randomness rather than to heat content.
walkthrough:
Visualise disorder**
Imagine a tidy crystal versus a gas spreading through a room. Entropy measures how spread out matter and energy are. More random arrangements and more dispersed energy mean higher entropy.
Final answer: Entropy is a measure of the disorder or randomness of a system.

hints: Apply $\Delta S^{\circ} = \sum S^{\circ}(\text{products}) - \sum S^{\circ}(\text{reactants})$ to $\text{NH}_2\text{Cl(g)} + \text{NH}_3\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{N}_2\text{H}_4\text{(g)} + \text{HCl(g)}$ using the table values.
walkthrough:
Set up products minus reactants**
For $\text{NH}_2\text{Cl(g)} + \text{NH}_3\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{N}_2\text{H}_4\text{(g)} + \text{HCl(g)}$:
$$\Delta S^{\circ} = [S^{\circ}(\text{N}_2\text{H}_4) + S^{\circ}(\text{HCl})] - [S^{\circ}(\text{NH}_2\text{Cl}) + S^{\circ}(\text{NH}_3)]$$

Substitute and evaluate**
$$\Delta S^{\circ} = (237 + 187) - (241 + 198) = 424 - 439 = -15.0 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$$
The small negative value makes sense because two gas moles give two gas moles with slightly less disorder.

hints: Use $\Delta H^{\circ} = \sum \Delta H_f^{\circ}(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta H_f^{\circ}(\text{reactants})$ with the $\Delta H_f^{\circ}$ values in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Write the formation expression**
$$\Delta H^{\circ} = [\Delta H_f^{\circ}(\text{N}_2\text{H}_4) + \Delta H_f^{\circ}(\text{HCl})] - [\Delta H_f^{\circ}(\text{NH}_2\text{Cl}) + \Delta H_f^{\circ}(\text{NH}_3)]$$

Insert numbers carefully with signs**
$$\Delta H^{\circ} = [95.4 + (-92.3)] - [80.1 + (-45.9)] = 3.1 - 34.2 = -31.1 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$
The reaction is exothermic.

hints: Recall the Gibbs equation $\Delta G^{\circ} = \Delta H^{\circ} - T\Delta S^{\circ}$ at $T = 298 \text{ K}$.
Convert $\Delta S^{\circ} = -15.0 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$ to $-0.015 \text{ kJ K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$ before multiplying by T to keep units consistent with $\Delta H^{\circ}$.
walkthrough:
Align the units**
$\Delta H^{\circ}$ is in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ but $\Delta S^{\circ}$ is in $\text{J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$. Convert:
$$-15.0 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1} = -0.015 \text{ kJ K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$$

Calculate $\Delta G^{\circ}$ at 298 K**
$$\Delta G^{\circ} = -31.1 - 298 \times (-0.015) = -31.1 + 4.47 = -26.6 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$
Negative $\Delta G^{\circ}$ means the reaction is feasible under standard conditions at 298 K.
Final answer: $$\Delta G^{\circ} = \Delta H^{\circ} - T\Delta S^{\circ} = -31.1 - (298 \times -0.015) = -26.6 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$

hints: Look at the sign of $\Delta S^{\circ}$ from (c)(ii) and consider how the $-T\Delta S^{\circ}$ term in $\Delta G^{\circ} = \Delta H^{\circ} - T\Delta S^{\circ}$ changes as T increases.
walkthrough:
Track the $-T\Delta S^{\circ}$ term**
Here $\Delta S^{\circ} = -15.0 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$. So $-T\Delta S^{\circ} = -T \times (\text{negative}) = +T \times 0.015$. As T grows, this positive contribution grows.

Link to feasibility**
$\Delta G^{\circ} = \text{negative } \Delta H^{\circ} + \text{increasing positive term}$. At higher T, $\Delta G^{\circ}$ becomes less negative and eventually positive, so the reaction becomes less feasible.

Final answer: Since $\Delta S^{\circ}$ is negative, as T increases $T\Delta S^{\circ}$ becomes more negative so $-T\Delta S^{\circ}$ becomes more positive and $\Delta G^{\circ}$ becomes more positive, less negative, hence less feasible.

hints: Rank ethylamine, ammonia and phenylamine by how available the nitrogen lone pair is for bonding to $\text{H}^+$.
Consider how an ethyl group pushes electron density toward N compared with H in ammonia.
Consider what happens to the N lone pair in phenylamine where the N p-orbital can interact with the benzene $\pi$ system.
Link all effects to the definition of a base as a proton acceptor and how electron density on N stabilises the conjugate acid.
walkthrough:
State the order and the test for basicity**
A base accepts $\text{H}^+$. The easier the N lone pair bonds to $\text{H}^+$, the stronger the base. The order is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2 > \text{NH}_3 > \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$.

Explain why ethylamine is strongest**
The ethyl group is electron donating by the positive inductive effect. It pushes electron density onto N, making the lone pair more negative and more readily donated to $\text{H}^+$. The ethylammonium ion is also better stabilised than $\text{NH}_4^+$.

Explain why phenylamine is weakest**
In phenylamine the lone pair on N sits in a p-orbital that overlaps with the delocalised $\pi$ system of the benzene ring. The lone pair is delocalised into the ring and is much less available to form a new $\text{N-H}$ bond. Protonation would destroy this delocalisation, so it is unfavourable.

Tie the comparison together**
Ammonia is the middle reference with no donating alkyl group and no delocalisation. So increased electron density raises basicity in ethylamine, while withdrawal of the lone pair into the ring lowers basicity in phenylamine.

Final answer: Basicity: ethylamine > ammonia > phenylamine.
Ethyl group is electron donating, increases electron density on N, lone pair more available to accept $\text{H}^+$.
In phenylamine the N lone pair is delocalised into the benzene $\pi$ ring system by overlap of N p-orbital with the ring, less available to accept $\text{H}^+$.
Basicity depends on ability of N to accept a proton.
